topic: L1.1 Hierarchy and Classification of the Number System
subject: Maths

concepts.name: Number System Hierarchy and Set Inclusion
concepts.description: The nested hierarchy of number sets (N, Z, Q, R, C), the correct proper-subset chain, the convention for whether 0 belongs to N, and the relationship between whole numbers and natural numbers.
core_skills: State the correct proper subset chain N subset Z subset Q subset R subset C.
Identify the irrational numbers as the set R \ Q and distinguish them from rationals.
Determine membership of 0 in N under the ISO 80000-2 convention and relate it to the whole numbers W = N union {0}.
Use set operations (subset, union, intersection, set difference, complement) to describe relationships between number sets.
Construct an algebraic comparison of N, Z, Q, R, C against the four basic operations (+, -, x, /) regarding closure.
prerequisites: Familiarity with natural numbers, integers, rational numbers and real numbers
Basic set notation and operations (element of, subset, union, intersection, set difference, complement)
misconceptions: That Z is a subset of N (integers inside naturals), as in the distractor Z subset N subset Q subset R subset C.
That Q comes before Z in the chain (N subset Q subset Z subset R subset C).
That R is a subset of Q (N subset Z subset R subset Q subset C).
That 0 is always excluded from the natural numbers regardless of convention.
That a set containing non-real elements (such as S union T where T = {x in C | x^2 + 4 = 0}) can be a subset of R or Q.
traps: The position of 0 in N depends on convention; under ISO 80000-2, 0 is in N, and W = N union {0} was introduced separately.
Proper subset ordering matters: Q must sit between Z and R, and C must be the outermost set.
A union that includes complex roots of x^2 + 4 = 0 (namely 2i and -2i) cannot lie inside R or Q.
concepts.depth_test: Explain why the whole numbers W = N union {0} were introduced even though 0 is included in N under ISO 80000-2, and justify why Q must be placed between Z and R in the chain N subset Z subset Q subset R subset C.

concepts.name: Closure Properties under Binary Operations
concepts.description: Whether a number set is closed under a given operation (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division), how to prove closure, and how to disprove it with a single counterexample.
core_skills: Determine whether sets such as N, Z, Q, R, the negative integers Z^-, the odd integers, the irrationals, the non-zero rationals, and sets of the form {a + b*sqrt(3)} are closed under +, -, x, /.
Disprove closure by providing one valid counterexample (for example (-2) x (-3) = 6 is not in Z^-).
Prove closure by showing the result remains in the set (for example rationalising the denominator of 1/(a + b*sqrt(3))).
Identify which specific set-operation pair fails closure (for example irrationals under addition, or Z \ N under subtraction).
Recognise that division by zero is undefined and identify the property it violates.
prerequisites: Number System Hierarchy and Set Inclusion
Rationalising surd denominators
Set membership and counterexample reasoning
misconceptions: That the irrational numbers are closed under addition (false, since sqrt(2) + (-sqrt(2)) = 0).
That the set Z \ N is closed under subtraction (for example 2 - 5 = -3 is not in Z \ N).
That the negative integers Z^- are closed under multiplication (the product of two negatives is positive).
That dividing by zero is a valid operation and that closure still holds.
That closure is judged on typical elements rather than on every possible pair of elements.
traps: Closure under one operation does not imply closure under another.
When testing closure under division, zero divisors must be excluded before the test is valid.
A single counterexample is sufficient to disprove closure, but proving closure requires a general argument.
The product of two irrationals can be rational (for example sqrt(2) x sqrt(2) = 2), so 'irrational times irrational is irrational' is false.
concepts.depth_test: Prove that Z^- is not closed under multiplication using a counterexample, then determine whether the odd integers ARE closed under multiplication and explain why.

concepts.name: Algebraic Structures: Fields, Identity and Inverse Elements
concepts.description: Field axioms and group-like properties: finding identity elements for arbitrary binary operations, deciding whether an identity exists, and computing additive and multiplicative inverses for rational and complex numbers.
core_skills: Find the identity element for a custom operation (for example for a*b = a + b - 5 the identity is 5, and for a*b = a + b + ab it is 0).
Determine whether an identity element exists for a given operation (for example a o b = a^2 + b^2 has no identity in R).
Compute additive and multiplicative inverses of complex numbers and use them to show Q and C are fields.
Explain why Z is not a field because it lacks multiplicative inverses except for +/-1.
Verify closure and associativity for a custom operation on a restricted set (G = R \ {-1}, a*b = a + b + ab).
Derive the inverse a^-1 = -a/(1 + a) for the operation a*b = a + b + ab and explain why a = -1 is excluded.
prerequisites: Closure Properties under Binary Operations
Arithmetic with fractions and complex numbers
Solving simple linear equations for an unknown identity element
misconceptions: That the identity element for a custom operation is always 0 or 1 (for a*b = a + b - 5 the identity is 5).
That every non-zero integer has a multiplicative inverse in Z.
That an identity element always exists for any binary operation (for a o b = a^2 + b^2 none exists).
That the non-zero integers Z* form a field with multiplicative inverses for every element.
Confusing the additive inverse with the multiplicative inverse of a complex number.
traps: The identity depends on the operation, not just the set; always solve a*e = a for e.
For a o b = a^2 + b^2, the natural candidate e = 0 fails because a^2 + 0 = a^2 is not equal to a in general.
Values that make a denominator zero (a = -1) must be excluded so the inverse exists.
The multiplicative inverse of a + bi requires dividing by a^2 + b^2, not simply flipping signs.
concepts.depth_test: For G = R \ {-1} with a*b = a + b + ab, prove closure and associativity, find the identity and the inverse a^-1, and explain why a = -1 must be excluded. Alternatively, explain why Q is a field but Z is not.

concepts.name: Rational vs Irrational Classification and Irrationality Proofs
concepts.description: Distinguishing rational from irrational numbers, placing a value in its most restrictive fundamental set, and proving irrationality by contradiction using the coprime assumption.
core_skills: Classify a number as natural, integer, rational, or irrational in its most restrictive fundamental set.
Recognise that expressions containing pi or surds can still be rational, e.g. (pi + 1)/(3pi + 3) = 1/3.
Prove that sqrt(2) is irrational by contradiction while stating the assumption gcd(a, b) = 1.
Use the closure of Q under arithmetic to prove that 3 + 2*sqrt(2) is irrational given that sqrt(2) is irrational.
Show a number is irrational by demonstrating its decimal is non-terminating and non-recurring.
Simplify surd products to find the most restrictive set, e.g. sqrt(12) x sqrt(3) = 6, which is in N.
prerequisites: Number System Hierarchy and Set Inclusion
Proof by contradiction
Coprime integers and the gcd
Basic surd manipulation
misconceptions: That any expression containing pi or a surd is automatically irrational (for example (pi + 1)/(3pi + 3) = 1/3, and sqrt(12) x sqrt(3) = 6).
That recurring or terminating decimals are irrational (they are rational).
That sqrt(2.25) is irrational (it equals 1.5).
That sqrt(2) + 1/sqrt(2) is rational (it is irrational).
That irrationality can be established just because an expression looks complicated without simplifying it.
traps: A fraction of surds or pi may reduce to a rational number, so it must be simplified before classification.
The 'most restrictive' set matters: a value may belong to N rather than merely to R \ Q.
In the contradiction proof, failing to state the coprime assumption gcd(a, b) = 1 breaks the argument.
Recurring decimals such as 0.345345... are rational, not irrational.
concepts.depth_test: Prove that sqrt(2) is irrational, explicitly stating the coprime assumption, then use that result to prove that 3 + 2*sqrt(2) is irrational. Alternatively, show why (pi + 1)/(3pi + 3) is rational despite containing pi.

concepts.name: Recurring Decimals and Rational Fraction Representation
concepts.description: Converting recurring and terminating decimals into exact irreducible fractions and understanding that decimal representations are not unique (for example 0.9 recurring equals 1).
core_skills: Convert a simple recurring decimal to a fraction (for example 0.27 recurring = 27/99 = 3/11).
Set up algebraic equations to convert a mixed recurring decimal such as 2.1 36 recurring into 47/22.
Add recurring decimals as fractions and reduce to lowest terms (for example 0.27 recurring + 0.18 recurring = 5/11).
Prove algebraically that 0.9 recurring equals 1 using 10x - x = 9.
Explain why any terminating decimal has two equivalent recurring representations.
Convert a recurring decimal in another base (0.4 recurring in base 5 equals 1 in base 5).
prerequisites: Rational vs Irrational Classification and Irrationality Proofs
Arithmetic with fractions
Place value and number-base representation
misconceptions: That 0.9 recurring is slightly less than 1.
That every recurring decimal has only one representation.
That 0.27 recurring + 0.18 recurring cannot simplify to a neat fraction (it equals 5/11).
That an answer like 45/99 is acceptable without reducing to lowest terms.
That the non-recurring prefix in a mixed recurring decimal can be ignored when setting up the algebra.
traps: For mixed recurring decimals, the multiplication must shift the non-recurring prefix as well as the recurring part (for example 2.1 36 recurring).
Final answers must be in lowest terms so that gcd(p, q) = 1.
Every terminating decimal has a dual repeating representation ending in trailing 9s.
The recurring-decimal-to-fraction technique generalises across bases, such as base 5.
concepts.depth_test: Prove algebraically that 0.9 recurring equals 1, and convert 2.1 36 recurring into an irreducible fraction showing the full algebraic setup and the reduction.

concepts.name: Density of Rational and Irrational Numbers on the Real Line
concepts.description: The density property of the rationals and irrationals on the real line, partitions of R into disjoint dense subsets, and constructing a number of a required type between two given numbers.
core_skills: State that between any two distinct real numbers there are infinitely many rationals and infinitely many irrationals.
Explain why the integers are not dense on the real line.
Construct an irrational number between two rationals, such as 0.121010010001... between 0.12 and 0.13.
Prove that R can be partitioned into two disjoint dense subsets A = Q and B = R \ Q.
Recognise when an equation has an empty real solution set (for example |x - 4| = -2).
prerequisites: Number System Hierarchy and Set Inclusion
Rational vs Irrational Classification and Irrationality Proofs
Recurring Decimals and Rational Fraction Representation
misconceptions: That between two distinct rationals there may be no irrational number.
That the integers are dense on the real line because every interval contains an integer.
That the irrationals are discrete points spaced at regular intervals.
That an absolute-value equation such as |x - 4| = -2 can have a real solution.
traps: Constructing an irrational between two rationals requires a non-terminating, non-recurring pattern, not just any arbitrary number.
Both Q and its complement R \ Q are dense, so a partition of R gives two dense subsets.
The empty set is a legitimate solution set, as in |x - 4| = -2.
concepts.depth_test: Show that 0.121010010001... lies strictly between 0.12 and 0.13 and is irrational, then explain how the density property applies to both A = Q and B = R \ Q in the partition of R.

concepts.name: Complex Numbers: Standard Form Arithmetic and Powers of i
concepts.description: Arithmetic with complex numbers written as a + bi, simplifying powers of i using the period-4 cycle, and solving equations by equating real and imaginary parts.
core_skills: Simplify powers of i using the period-4 cycle (for example i^15 + i^22 + i^101 = -1).
Evaluate expressions involving powers of (1 + i) and (1 - i) together with the square root of a negative number.
Solve complex linear equalities by equating real and imaginary parts (for example 2x - 3y = 7 and x + 4y = -2).
Solve quadratic equations with complex roots (for example z^2 + 2z + 5 = 0 gives z = -1 +/- 2i).
Apply i^2 = -1 and write sqrt(-k) as i*sqrt(k).
prerequisites: Necessity of Complex Numbers (Extension of the Real System)
Arithmetic with surds
Simultaneous linear equations
misconceptions: That large powers of i must be computed directly rather than reduced modulo 4.
That sqrt(-25) = -5 rather than 5i.
Mixing up real and imaginary parts when equating the two sides of a complex equality.
Making sign errors when cycling through powers of i.
traps: Exponents must be reduced modulo 4 (for example i^101 = i^(4 x 25 + 1) = i).
A rational real term from (1 + i)^4/(1 - i)^2 must be combined with the imaginary part of sqrt(-25).
Extraneous solutions can appear if real and imaginary parts are not matched correctly.
concepts.depth_test: Compute (1 + i)^4 / (1 - i)^2 + sqrt(-25) and state its real part, explaining each simplification step. Alternatively, solve (2x - 3y) + (x + 4y)i = 7 - 2i by equating real and imaginary parts.

concepts.name: Complex Numbers: Modulus, Argument, Polar Form and Geometry
concepts.description: Geometric representation of complex numbers on the Argand plane, including modulus, principal argument, polar form, distance between points, and conjugate relationships.
core_skills: Compute the modulus |z| = sqrt(a^2 + b^2).
Compute the principal argument Arg(z) in the interval (-pi, pi], accounting for the quadrant (for example -1 - i*sqrt(3) has Arg = -2pi/3).
Convert a complex number to polar form r(cos theta + i sin theta), for example -16i = 16(cos(-pi/2) + i sin(-pi/2)).
Calculate the distance between two points on the complex plane as |z1 - z2|.
Plot complex roots on an Argand diagram and describe their geometric relationship, such as complex conjugates.
Find the moduli and arguments of conjugate-pair solutions (for example z^2 + 2z + 5 = 0 gives |z| = sqrt(5)).
prerequisites: Complex Numbers: Standard Form Arithmetic and Powers of i
Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry
Coordinate geometry on the Cartesian plane
misconceptions: Choosing the wrong quadrant for the argument because the signs of a and b are ignored.
Reporting an argument outside the interval (-pi, pi].
Treating the argument of a pure imaginary number as 0 or pi instead of +/-pi/2.
Omitting the modulus r and writing only cos theta + i sin theta as the polar form.
Confusing the complex conjugate a - bi with the multiplicative inverse.
traps: The principal argument interval (-pi, pi] excludes pi except at the negative real axis.
For the pure imaginary -16i, r = 16 and theta = -pi/2.
Distance between points uses |z1 - z2|, not the sum.
Complex conjugates are reflections in the real axis with equal modulus and opposite arguments.
concepts.depth_test: Find the modulus and principal argument of z = -1 - i*sqrt(3), explain how the quadrant determines the correct Arg(z), and write its polar form.

concepts.name: Necessity of Complex Numbers (Extension of the Real System)
concepts.description: The fundamental limitation of the real number system that motivates constructing the complex numbers, namely that negative real numbers have no real square root, and how C removes this deficiency.
core_skills: Explain that the square root of a negative real number is undefined in R.
Recognise that equations such as x^2 + 4 = 0 have no real solutions and that their solutions lie in C.
State that a negative value has no real square root.
Identify that sets such as {x in C | x^2 + 4 = 0} contain non-real elements.
prerequisites: Number System Hierarchy and Set Inclusion
misconceptions: That every polynomial equation must have real solutions.
That sqrt(-1) is undefined absolutely, rather than undefined in R and defined as i in C.
That an absolute-value equation such as |x - 4| = -2 has a real solution.
traps: Distinguishing 'no solution in R' from 'no solution at all' - the solution may exist in C.
Equations with a negative discriminant produce complex conjugate roots rather than real roots.
concepts.depth_test: Explain why x^2 + 4 = 0 has no real solution but does have solutions in C, state those solutions, and explain why the complex number set was constructed to extend R.
